details:
**Mother Courage and Her Children**
Brecht's most famous play (1939), set during the Thirty Years' War. Anna Fierling, nicknamed Mother Courage, pulls a canteen wagon behind the armies and sells supplies to soldiers, profiting from the war that takes all three of her children. It is the most common title clue and the usual giveaway for Brecht.

**Eilif, Swiss Cheese, and Kattrin**
Mother Courage's three children, all of whom die over the course of the play. Early on she foretells that brave Eilif will die for his bravery, honest Swiss Cheese for his honesty (he is shot after hiding the regiment's paybox), and kind Kattrin for her kindness.

**Kattrin beating the drum on the roof**
The climax of Mother Courage. The mute girl Kattrin climbs onto a roof and beats a drum to wake the town of Halle and warn it of an approaching Catholic army, and the soldiers shoot her. Afterward Mother Courage sings a lullaby over her body and keeps pulling the wagon.

**The Threepenny Opera**
Brecht's 1928 "play with music," written with composer Kurt Weill and adapted from John Gay's The Beggar's Opera. Set in London, it follows the criminal Macheath ("Mack the Knife"), who marries Polly Peachum. Her father Jeremiah Peachum, boss of the city's beggars, tries to get Macheath hanged.

**"Mack the Knife" and "Pirate Jenny"**
The two most famous songs from The Threepenny Opera, with Brecht's lyrics. "Mack the Knife" opens the play by comparing Macheath's knife to the "pearly white" teeth of a shark. In "Pirate Jenny," a barmaid dreams of a "Black Freighter" with eight sails and fifty cannons that will destroy the town that mistreats her.

**Tiger Brown**
London's chief of police in The Threepenny Opera and Macheath's old army comrade from the colonial wars. Together they sing the "Cannon Song." Peachum threatens to have Brown fired by sending a crowd of beggars to disrupt Queen Victoria's coronation unless Macheath is arrested.

**Distancing effect (alienation effect, Verfremdungseffekt)**
Brecht's core theatrical idea. Bare sets, songs, placards, and stylized acting keep the audience from identifying emotionally with the characters so that they think critically about what they see. He developed it partly in an essay on Chinese acting and in "A Short Organum for the Theater."

**Epic theater**
The name of Brecht's Marxist dramatic style, which puts political argument ahead of illusion and catharsis. Related terms that appear in clues include gestus (a gesture showing a character's social attitude, such as Mother Courage's "silent scream"), the "Not/But" element, and his didactic "learning-plays" (Lehrstücke).

**The Caucasian Chalk Circle**
Brecht's play inspired by the Chinese drama The Chalk Circle by Li Xingdao. The servant girl Grusha rescues and raises Michael, the baby the Governor's wife abandoned during a revolt, and escapes to the Northern Mountains while the Ironshirts chase her. The rogue judge Azdak places the child in a chalk circle. Grusha refuses to pull him out for fear of hurting him, so Azdak awards her the child.

**The Good Person of Szechwan**
Brecht's parable play, also translated as The Good Woman of Setzuan. Three gods, guided by the water seller Wang, reward the kind prostitute Shen Teh with money that she uses to buy a tobacco shop. To protect herself from freeloaders she disguises herself as her ruthless male cousin Shui Ta. She falls in love with Yang Sun, an unemployed pilot who exploits her.

**Yvette Pottier and the "Song of Fraternization"**
The camp prostitute in Mother Courage. She sings the "Song of Fraternization" about her first love, an enemy cook, and later marries a colonel. Kattrin is fascinated by her red high-heeled boots.

**"Song of the Great Capitulation" and the Chaplain**
In this song from Mother Courage, the title character talks a young soldier out of making an angry complaint. The Chaplain, who chops wood after the war turns against his side, laments that he "studied to be a pastor of souls," and the cook (Lamb) is another camp follower.

**The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui**
Brecht's 1941 satire of Hitler's rise to power, retold as the story of a Chicago gangster who seizes control of the cauliflower trade by running a protection racket on the Cauliflower Trust.

**Life of Galileo**
Brecht's play about the astronomer. Galileo passes off a telescope as his own invention, presenting it to the Venetian Arsenal (in a red leather casing instead of green), and later recants his beliefs before the Inquisition, which disappoints his student Andrea Sarti. While under house arrest he secretly writes the Discorsi (Discourses), and Andrea smuggles it out of Italy at the end.

**Saint Joan of the Stockyards, Mahagonny, and Baal**
Other Brecht works. In Saint Joan of the Stockyards, Joan Dark of the Black Straw Hats (a Salvation Army-type group) confronts the meatpacking king Pierpont Mauler in Chicago. Rise and Fall of the City of Mahagonny, another collaboration with Weill, features the "Alabama Song" ("show us the way to the next whiskey bar") and the lumberjack Jimmy Mahoney. Baal, his early first play, follows a dissolute poet who seduces women and murders his friend Ekhart.
